# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review of the Varden–Halden 24-Month Follow-up

This report does what the earlier exchange called for:

- **It measures persistence directly.** It follows the controlled stratum to 24 months instead of inferring durability from comparisons between different studies.
- **It checks unrecorded work.** A second, independent hours measure tests the timesheet concern raised at nine months.
- **It tests the meetings hypothesis under a registered plan.** The mediation analysis was filed before the 24-month outcomes were available.
- **It answers both published claims fairly.** It rebuts the "entirely an artifact" claim and the "no decay" claim on the evidence, and concedes what each got right.
- **It treats the Halden subset cautiously.** The phrase "survivors twice over" is the right way to describe it.
- **It reports the counter arm's termination plainly**, including a costing, which the nine-month report lacked.

The main conclusion is well supported: the per-hour gain in case-processing declined but persisted at 24 months.

There are five problems:

1. Two control offices changed their practices mid-trial. This bears directly on the decay estimate, and the report does not connect the two.
2. The scope of the "system log" hours measure is undefined, and the Summary compares a timesheet figure with a log figure.
3. The mediation result is partly built into how output per hour is defined, re-tests the offices that generated the hypothesis, and is overstated as "confirms".
4. Outcomes requested at nine months, especially backlog, are still missing.
5. Some details of the Halden subset don't reconcile with earlier figures.

## Arithmetic check

The core figures hold:

| Figure | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Output per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% |
| Output per hour, system logs | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% |
| Change in meeting hours | treated −3.5 h, control −0.2 h | −3.3 h |
| Halden hours (11 organisations) | 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% |
| Halden output per hour | 0.968 / 0.866 | +11.8% |

The mediation shares sum to 100% (47 + 18 + 35). The 3.3-hour fall in meeting time matches the nine-month exploratory difference, which is reassuring.

Three statements don't match the numbers:

- **The Summary compares different measures.** It says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data". But 12.5% was measured with timesheets, and no log data exist for nine months. The comparable decline is 12.5% → 9.8% on timesheets, a fall of about 22%. Going from 12.5% to 8.5% overstates the decline at about 32%.
- **"About a quarter" (§5) is imprecise.** It sits between those two figures. Specify the measure: "about a fifth, on timesheets".
- **The decline is not statistically established.** The nine- and 24-month intervals overlap heavily: +6.9 to +18.4 at nine months, +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months. "Consistent with some fading" is the right wording, and the Summary's "the gain has therefore declined" should be equally careful.

## 1. The meeting audit affects the control group and the decay estimate

From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their recurring meetings, and their output per hour then rose 4.1% against their own previous six months. The report treats this as an interesting side observation. It is also **contamination of the control arm**, and it biases the 24-month difference-in-differences estimate downward.

As a rough illustration, assume equal office sizes and that the 24-month estimate reflects the period after month 15. Then two of seven offices improving by about 4% lowers the treatment effect by roughly 1 percentage point. That is a substantial part of the 2.7-point decline from 12.5% to 9.8%. Some of the measured "fading" may be the control group improving rather than the treated offices slipping.

Needed:

- **A sensitivity analysis excluding the two offices**, or restricting control data to the period before month 15.
- **The timing and window of the 24-month estimate.** State whether it uses month 24 alone, months 13–24, or the whole period.
- **Whether the audit was prompted by the nine-month report.** If the offices read the published meetings finding and acted on it, the trial's own results contaminated its control group. That is worth stating, because it will happen in any trial that publishes interim results.

The broader point in §3 is fair: part of the gain may be available without reducing hours. It is suitably hedged.

## 2. The system-log hours measure needs defining

"Active log-in time on the county's case-management system" can mean different things, and the interpretation depends on which:

- **If logs cover only time spent on the case system**, they exclude meetings, email and phone work. In that case:
  - log hours and timesheet hours measure different things, and a smaller percentage fall on logs does not show that logs record "slightly more work";
  - output per log hour is output per hour of case work, which changes the meaning of the mediation result (point 3);
  - work done outside the case system is still unrecorded, so the log measure does not settle the unrecorded-work concern.
- **If logs count all time logged in, including idle time and time in meetings**, the measure includes time that is not work.

The figures suggest the first reading is unlikely. If logs excluded meetings, the 3.3-hour fall in meeting time would make log hours fall much less than timesheet hours, not by a similar 11%. But this should be stated, not left to inference.

Please report **levels**, not only percentage changes, for both measures in both arms. Then readers can see how much work timesheets miss.

## 3. The mediation result is partly mechanical, not independent, and overstated

**Part of the effect is built into the outcome.** If the hours denominator includes meeting time, then removing meetings while case output stays the same raises output per hour by arithmetic alone. In that case the 47% share partly restates how the outcome is defined. If logs exclude meetings, a 47% share is a much stronger finding: fewer meetings would be making case-work time itself more productive, perhaps through fewer interruptions or longer uninterrupted blocks. The report should say which applies. The two readings support quite different conclusions.

**It is not an independent replication.** The test was registered at month 11, after the exploratory finding. It uses the same seven treated offices, and if the outcome window includes months 1–9, it partly reuses the data that suggested the hypothesis. It is a correctly pre-specified test, and that is valuable. But it does not answer the concern that a finding from seven offices may not replicate. Only a new set of offices could do that. ("Selected after results were known" was an inaccurate description of the original analysis, and the report is right to correct it.)

**The precision may be overstated.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds observations, but they are not independent. The effective sample is still 14 offices. The report should state how clustering was handled in the mediation model. With 14 clusters, an interval of 28–66% for the meetings share looks narrow, and small-cluster or bootstrap inference would show whether it holds.

**Mediators were not randomised.** The meeting cuts were a consequence of the treatment, not assigned. Offices whose managers cut meetings most may differ in other ways that affect output, such as manager quality. The Limitations section notes this assumption. The Summary's "confirms" ignores it, and "supports" would be accurate.

## 4. Outcomes still missing

Several items raised about the nine-month report are not addressed, and some matter more at 24 months:

- **Backlog and case age.** The nine-month report's own Limitations asked "whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines". Two years is exactly when that would show. Report backlog size, the age of open cases, and the share decided within deadline, by arm.
- **Cases received by arm**, to rule out work being redirected from treated to control offices.
- **Sick days per scheduled day**, and whether the 30-hour week was four days or five shorter days. The −27% cannot be interpreted without this.
- **Quality and resignations as difference-in-differences estimates with intervals.** At present they are still levels for each arm. Appeal overturns at 3.2% vs 3.0% are probably fine, but they should be estimated the same way as the other outcomes.

## 5. The Halden subset: details that don't reconcile

- **Source of hours data.** Of the 23 organisations with output records, only 17 also had time tracking. Are all 11 continuing organisations among those 17? If not, where do their actual hours come from?
- **The baseline matches a different subset exactly.** The 11 have baseline hours of 40.3, the same as Varga & Holm's 27-organisation time-tracking subset. Their 17-organisation subset had 40.4. It may be a coincidence, but it should be checked.
- **No comparison with six months.** The 11.8% here and the 10.8% in Varga & Holm come from different subsets. Nothing about change over time can be inferred from them, and the report rightly doesn't try. A sentence saying so would stop readers from making that comparison.
- **The marketing agency does not fit the description.** The Summary groups all three reversions as having "client-facing or coverage obligations". The marketing agency cited client deadlines, which is deadline-driven work and would be coded discretionary in the meta-analysis. That makes it a reversion in discretionary work, which complicates the clean split between work types. It is worth stating honestly.
- **Non-response.** Nine of 23 organisations declined. If any of them reverted, the reversion rate of 3 in 14 understates the true figure.

## 6. Authorship and independence

R. Okafor, an author of the original Halden paper, co-authors the Halden follow-up and a section rebutting the main critique of that paper. The Varden authors similarly assess the critique of their own meetings hypothesis. Neither fact invalidates the analysis, but both should be stated in a competing-interests note. Sharing the Halden follow-up data with Varga & Holm would be a strong way to show good faith.

## 7. §5, response to earlier claims

**The response to the "entirely an artifact" claim is sound.** The case-processing estimate meets the re-analysis's standards: records, actual hours, randomisation and at least 18 months of follow-up. One qualification: the re-analysis also recommended analysing everything that was enrolled, and the 24-month result covers only the stratum that kept going. The rebuttal holds for its specific claim, that no per-hour gain remains. But the trial as a whole does not support adopting reduced hours across all the work types it tested.

**The response to the meta-analysis is correct and important.** If all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, that is exactly the confounding I suggested might be present. The Varden figures, with the contamination caveat from point 1, are now the best evidence on decay. It would help to name the four studies.

## Suggested revision of the Summary's key sentences

> In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control was 9.8% at 24 months on timesheets (12.5% at nine months) and 8.5% on system logs; output per employee was −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2). The gain has declined somewhat but remains clearly above zero; part of the decline may reflect two control offices independently cutting meetings from month 15. A registered mediation analysis, conducted in the same offices that generated the hypothesis, attributes 47% (28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain to reduced meeting time and 18% (2 to 34%) to reduced fatigue, under the assumption of no unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding.

Taken together, the five documents now support a fairly clear picture:

- **Per-hour gains** in discretionary work are real but closer to 8–10% than 20%+.
- **The gain shrinks only modestly** over two years in the one controlled study that measured it.
- **A large share of the gain comes from cutting meetings** and other reorganisation, not rest alone. Whether that can be captured without cutting hours is the obvious next trial.
- **Coverage-bound work loses output per employee.** Keeping service levels requires more staff.
